title: The letter A
hook: Shingon meditation on the Sanskrit letter A, the sound of all beginnings

segments.voice: Yesterday, the two mandalas, womb and diamond. Your line was two worlds. Where did two opposites meet for you? Today, Shingon shrinks the whole map down to a single letter. Day one thousand three hundred forty-one.

Ah. Open your mouth and let the breath out, and that's the sound that comes. No tongue against teeth, no lips pressing. Babies make it. Doctors ask for it with a little wooden stick. People sigh it when the hot bath is just right. It might be the plainest sound a person can make. Shingon took that sound, and the letter that writes it, and set it at the center of a meditation: a single letter on a white moon, on a lotus. That letter is today's word: A.
screen: `AH: THE PLAINEST SOUND.` → `NO TONGUE, NO LIPS.` → `A LETTER ON A MOON.`

segments.voice: First, the letter. Shingon teachers point out that in the Indian alphabet A stands first, and that every consonant is read with a hidden a sound after it unless a mark silences it. So the A, they say, is in every sound, the way the open breath is underneath every word. Second, what the letter stands for. The Mahavairocana Sutra, which Shingon treasures, links the letter A with the teaching that all things are unborn from the beginning. Shingon reads it this way: before any thing appears, before any word is shaped, there is an origin that was never made and never ends. The A points to it. So the plainest sound becomes a sign for the ground of everything. Third, the practice. Shingon calls it ajikan, contemplation of the letter A. Tradition associates it with Kukai's school, and the image is simple. A lotus. On the lotus, a full moon disc, white and round. On the moon, the letter A, written in an old Indian script. The practitioner gazes at the image, breathes, and lets the sound and the shape of A fill the mind, until the moon seems to grow, and the letter with it. Fourth, why so small. Yesterday's mandalas were crowded with buddhas, a whole world painted. Today's is one letter. In Shingon, both carry the whole teaching. The vast map and the single sound are not two, the way the womb world and the diamond world are not two. A person who can't take in a whole mandala can still breathe out ah.
screen: `A COMES FIRST, AND HIDES IN ALL.` · `UNBORN FROM THE BEGINNING.` · `A LOTUS, A MOON, A LETTER.` · `THE WHOLE MAP IN ONE SOUND.` · then, large: `AH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe the sound ah. Sit comfortably and take a slow breath in. On the out-breath, let the sound come, quietly or only in your mind: ah. Don't push it. Let it be as long as the breath is, and no longer. Then breathe in again, and again, ah. If you'd like, picture a round white moon in front of you as you do it. If you lose the sound, start the next breath fresh. Nothing to get right. Just the open breath. The bell holds the time.
The letter A. In Shingon, the first letter and the sound inside every sound, a sign that all things are unborn from the beginning, and the heart of ajikan. Today's word.
Your line: ah. Today, when you notice the breath is held, let one long ah go out, aloud or silent. Day one thousand three hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Shingon practitioners practice ajikan, contemplating the Siddham letter A on a moon disc above a lotus while breathing and sounding A; it is also taught to lay people as an introduction to Shingon meditation.

original.note: Sanskrit a, the first letter. Shingon pictures it in the older Siddham script; this is the Devanagari form.

notes: Editor pass: screen no longer calls the letter golden (the voice and sources say only a letter on a white moon); facts about the alphabet now credited to Shingon teachers; varied the hook's closing formula; softened 'often taught to lay people'.
'A comes first' in Indic alphabets and the inherent a in consonants are facts about Brahmi-derived scripts; confirm the phrasing.
The Mahavairocana Sutra's teaching on the letter A as 'originally unborn' (adyanutpada) is paraphrased; confirm.

Ajikan's attribution to Kukai is given as 'tradition associates it with Kukai's school'; confirm the description of the image (letter on a moon disc on a lotus) and whether the letter is described as golden.
'Often taught to lay people' in howItsDone: confirm or soften.
Original: Devanagari अ given; the Siddham form is what Shingon uses. Confirm.
